notice: Owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. The structured source ledger, access classifications, language route and starter-reading notes are retained; no personal numerical scores are set.
method: Owner-supplied Top 250 synthesis across Greek and Roman primary works and selected later reception. The report’s merit order is retained in both views pending a separately reasoned reading-value order.

entries.standing: Position 1 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. The central reference point for Greek heroic poetry: anger, mortality, honour, pity and the costs of collective violence. Its literary richness and extensive afterlives make it the most generative foundation.
entries.reading: WHOLE: all 24 books; learn the Trojan War background first. A first sampling may use books 1, 6, 9, 16, 18, 22 and 24.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 2 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Foundational for narrative, recognition, hospitality and homecoming. Its competing storytellers and troubled restoration of a household reward reading beyond its famous adventures.
entries.reading: WHOLE: all 24 books. Begin here before rank 1 if a stronger narrative invitation helps.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 3 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Reworks Homer into an argument about migration, empire and sacrifice. Essential for understanding Roman claims to the past and the ethical tensions within Augustan literature.
entries.reading: WHOLE: all 12 books, after some Homer and a short account of Rome's civil wars.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 4 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Connects justice, education, psychology, metaphysics, poetry and political power. Its breadth and resistance to easy agreement give it exceptional educational value.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 1–4, 6–7 and 10; then the whole dialogue. Read Apology first.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 5 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. The richest single Roman poetic network of Greek and Roman myths. Narrative ingenuity and unstable perspectives make it indispensable for art, literature and the study of power.
entries.reading: WHOLE: all 15 books; use the index to track stories. A first sample is books 1, 3, 6 and 10.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 6 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. An integrated dramatic exploration of inherited violence, justice and civic institutions. The three plays illuminate one another and should not be reduced to a reassuring progress narrative.
entries.reading: WHOLE: the three surviving plays in the order named; read the family history of Atreus first.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 7 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Makes historical inquiry an encounter with competing testimony, cultural difference and human reversals. Its Persian, Egyptian and other perspectives complicate a narrowly Athenian education.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 1–2 and 7–9, then books 3–6. Events range from legendary antecedents to 479 BCE.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 8 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A demanding school in causation, political speech, war and the breakdown of norms. Its analysis is powerful but must be read as an authored interpretation.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: 1.1–23; 2.34–65; 3.36–85; 5.84–116; books 6–7. Then read all eight books. Narrative covers 431–411 BCE.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 9 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. The major ancient account of flourishing, habituation, deliberation, friendship and contemplation. It teaches distinctions that remain productive even where its social assumptions require criticism.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 1–3, 6, 8–10; then 4–5 and 7. Read slowly, reconstructing arguments.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 10 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. An exceptionally compact encounter with kinship, burial, civic authority and responsibility. Its varied political afterlives make it an ideal text for comparing interpretation with appropriation.
entries.reading: WHOLE; know the deaths of Eteocles and Polyneices. No need to read the other Theban plays first.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 11 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A masterpiece of recognition, dramatic irony and investigation. It sharpens distinctions between knowledge, intention and responsibility without depending on modern psychological readings.
entries.reading: WHOLE; follow each new piece of testimony rather than treating the plot as a riddle alone.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 12 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Explores divine power, religious experience, gender and the fragility of civic control. It resists a simple opposition between enlightened reason and irrational faith.
entries.reading: WHOLE; read a short introduction to Dionysus and tragic performance.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 13 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. The clearest entrance into Socratic inquiry and the conflict between philosophical integrity and public judgment. Its accessibility increases its educational value without making it a neutral trial transcript.
entries.reading: WHOLE; the trial represented occurred in 399 BCE.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 14 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Unites atomist explanation, therapy for fear and extraordinary poetry. It shows that ancient philosophy concerns nature and society as well as personal conduct.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 1, 3 and 5; then all six books. Pair with Epicurus's Letter to Menoeceus.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 15 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Stages rival accounts of love through myth, comedy, philosophical argument and personal testimony. It is a particularly rich introduction to the literary form of philosophy.
entries.reading: WHOLE; the dramatic gathering is set in 416 BCE, not the composition period.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 16 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Provides a central ancient ordering of divine succession and the origins of power. It is foundational mythic evidence, while remaining one poet's arrangement of varied traditions.
entries.reading: WHOLE, with a family tree and notes; do not memorise every name before continuing.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 17 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Exposes the range of Roman poetic selves, from invective and intimate grief to learned myth. Its Greek adaptations make literary reception visible inside antiquity.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: poems 1–5, 8, 11, 16, 31, 51, 64, 68, 70, 72, 85 and 101; then the collection.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 18 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Transforms Greek lyric into Roman meditations on friendship, pleasure, civic life and poetic survival. Reading private and public poems together prevents a merely aphoristic interpretation.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 19 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A powerful study of betrayal, exile, rhetoric and revenge. It creates a searching encounter with a foreign woman's vulnerability and the limits of sympathy.
entries.reading: WHOLE, after a brief account of Jason and the Argonauts.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 20 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A foundational comparative laboratory for character and political action. Its Greek–Roman pairings and enormous reception matter more educationally than reading every life consecutively.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: Alexander–Caesar; Demosthenes–Cicero; Pericles–Fabius Maximus, including surviving comparisons. Lives concern much earlier people.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 21 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Examines constitutions, citizenship, education and the relation between household and city. Its defence of hierarchy should be studied critically alongside its enduring analytical distinctions.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 1, 3–4 and 7–8; then 2, 5–6. Nicomachean Ethics book 1 helps.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 22 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Brings Greek ethical debate into Roman public and private obligations. Its treatment of apparent advantage versus right action became a major language of later moral argument.
entries.reading: WHOLE, with special attention to books 1 and 3; consult notes on late republican institutions.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 23 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Transforms classical rhetoric and Platonism through Christian self-examination. Memory, time and interpretation make it more than a conversion narrative.
entries.reading: WHOLE: all 13 books; first read books 1–9 if necessary, then return for 10–13. The life narrated is earlier than composition.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 24 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A foundational analysis of plot, imitation and tragic effect. Its usefulness depends on comparing its claims with actual plays rather than treating it as a universal rulebook.
entries.reading: WHOLE surviving text, after Oedipus the King and at least one other tragedy.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 25 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Essential for desire, song, address and the limits of survival. Reading damaged texts teaches how editorial reconstruction shapes the apparent ancient voice.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: fragments 1, 16, 31, 44, 94 and 96 in standard Voigt numbering; then all translated remains in an annotated edition.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 26 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Central to Roman historical memory, exemplary storytelling and republican identity. Its retrospective foundation stories demand comparison with archaeological and other evidence.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 1–2 and 21–22; then 5 and 30. Surviving books are 1–10 and 21–45; the original narrative extended to 9 BCE.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 27 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. An indispensable analysis of domination, elite complicity and the difficulty of truthful history. Its artistry should sharpen, rather than replace, source criticism.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 1, 4 and 14–16, as preserved; then all surviving books. Events concern 14–68 CE.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 28 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Offers a counterweight to aristocratic epic through labour, justice, household survival and seasonal knowledge. Its myths make moral and economic arguments concrete.
entries.reading: WHOLE, using notes for the calendar and agricultural passages.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 29 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Provides a durable framework for argument, character, emotion and style. It is most valuable when used to analyse an actual ancient speech.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: 1.1–3; 2.1–11; 3.1–12. Then the whole work; pair with Demosthenes or Cicero.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 30 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Combines the death of Socrates with arguments about soul, knowledge and philosophical life. It teaches sympathetic reconstruction without requiring assent to its conclusions.
entries.reading: WHOLE, after Apology and Crito; dramatic date 399 BCE.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 31 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A major statement of the orator's relation to knowledge, ethics and public life. Its expansive ideal helps connect the literary and intellectual strands of this list.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: 1.16–73; 2.178–216; 3.19–95. Then all three books.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 32 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Turns ethical reasoning into a varied literary relationship with a reader. Useful for attention, mortality, friendship and the contradictions of philosophy under imperial power.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: letters 1, 2, 7, 12, 28, 47, 71, 76, 83 and 104; then expand across the collection.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 33 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Reveals how myth, athletic victory, patronage and communal memory interact. Its difficulty is justified by the distinctively public conception of lyric it preserves.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: Olympian 1, 2 and 7; Pythian 1, 4 and 8; Nemean 5; Isthmian 8. Use a mythological commentary.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 34 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Preserves Stoicism as an active practice of questioning judgments and commitments. Its dramatic teaching voice prevents ethics from becoming a list of isolated slogans.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: 1.1, 1.18; 2.5, 2.10; 3.2, 3.22; 4.1. Then the four surviving books.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 35 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Combines adventure with leadership, collective decision-making and cultural encounter. It is accessible while allowing close scrutiny of an author's defence of his own role.
entries.reading: WHOLE: seven books; the expedition and retreat occurred in 401–399 BCE.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 36 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Explains Rome's Mediterranean ascendancy through connected history, institutions and causation. Essential for moving beyond isolated Greek and Roman narratives.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 1, 3 and the surviving portions of book 6; then the surviving fragments of book 38. The historical span ultimately reaches 146 BCE.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 37 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Uses cultivation and labour to think about knowledge, violence, loss and renewal. It makes Roman poetry's intellectual range visible beyond national epic.
entries.reading: WHOLE: four books, with agricultural notes; read book 4's Aristaeus and Orpheus narratives particularly closely.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 38 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A uniquely vivid ancient debate about poetry's civic value. Its literary contest becomes much richer after some Aeschylus and Euripides.
entries.reading: WHOLE, after Oresteia and one Euripidean tragedy.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 39 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Places persuasion, power and the good life in direct conflict. The changing interlocutors reveal why an ethical dispute cannot always be settled by verbal victory.
entries.reading: WHOLE, after Apology; Aristotle's Rhetoric is a useful later comparison.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 40 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Connects love, soul, persuasive speech and the risks of writing. Essential for thinking about what reading can and cannot do as education.
entries.reading: WHOLE, after Symposium and an introductory account of Plato's Forms.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 41 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Shows a Roman ruler repeatedly working on judgment and conduct. Educationally valuable when read as situated exercises, with both Stoic commitments and imperial responsibilities in view.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 2, 4, 6 and 12; then all 12 books. Read Epictetus first if possible.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 42 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A short, foundational argument about pleasure, desire, death and practical judgment. Especially valuable as a counterweight to the modern dominance of Stoic reading lists.
entries.reading: WHOLE; preserved in Diogenes Laertius 10.122–135.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 43 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Its declared inventions expose the conventions of travel writing, ethnography and epic. A lively lesson in how ancient readers could question authoritative narratives.
entries.reading: WHOLE: two books; some Odyssey helps identify the jokes.
entries.caveat: Commentary/reference support; see the ledger for scholarly, specialist, abstract or tertiary access limits. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 44 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A major surviving Latin experiment in curiosity, narrative framing, sexuality and religious transformation. Its mixture of comedy and devotion complicates modern genre expectations.
entries.reading: WHOLE: eleven books. Cupid and Psyche, 4.28–6.24, is an inviting first selection.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 45 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. The fullest surviving Roman account of rhetorical formation, including reading, imitation, argument and ethical aspiration. It explains an ancient educational ideal without defining a modern equivalent.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: 1.1–3; 2.2; 10.1–3; 12.1. Then consult other books around actual speeches.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 46 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Creates a Roman pastoral world shaped by dispossession, song contests and literary rivalry. A short foundation for later European pastoral and its political ambiguities.
entries.reading: WHOLE: ten eclogues; begin with 1, 4, 6 and 10 if needed.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 47 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Satirises education, debt and new intellectual fashions. Its caricature of Socrates provides a revealing comparison with Plato's defence of philosophical inquiry.
entries.reading: WHOLE, alongside Apology; do not treat the comic Socrates as reliable biography.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 48 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Makes desire, dependency and poetic identity compete with Roman public values. The fourth book expands elegy into myth and civic memory.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 49 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Revoices inherited myth through abandoned and disputing lovers. It provides a particularly direct exercise in comparing epic narrative with the perspective of a character inside it.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: letters 1, 7, 10 and 12; then 16–17. Read relevant Homeric, Virgilian and Medea material first.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 50 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. An exceptional transformation of Virgil, classical underworlds, ethics and poetic authority within medieval Christianity. Included as an active reconfiguration of antiquity, not evidence for ancient beliefs.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: Inferno 1–5 and 26; Purgatorio 21–22 and 30; Paradiso 6. Then the whole poem. Aeneid 6 is the key prerequisite.
entries.caveat: Commentary/reference support; see the ledger for scholarly, specialist, abstract or tertiary access limits. English translation by default. O-optional: Italian for study of the original; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 51 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. The central surviving development of late antique Platonism, addressing beauty, soul, intellect and unity. Essential for understanding Augustine and later Arabic, Jewish and Christian philosophy.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: I.6 On Beauty; I.2 On Virtues; IV.8 On the Descent of the Soul; V.1 On the Three Primary Hypostases; VI.9 On the Good or the One. Read Plato first.
entries.caveat: Commentary/reference support; see the ledger for scholarly, specialist, abstract or tertiary access limits. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 52 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Everyday conversation becomes an exploration of appetite, status and self-deception. It offers a different Roman literary education from epic grandeur and political declamation.
entries.caveat: Tertiary-reference support only in this audit; detailed scholarly cross-checking remains a gap. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 53 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Stages the collision of military necessity, deception and care for an abandoned sufferer. Its ethical argument is inseparable from dramatic relationships.
entries.reading: WHOLE; know who Odysseus, Neoptolemus and Philoctetes are.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 54 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Explores desire, chastity, shame and competing divine powers. It is indispensable preparation for Seneca's and Racine's different Phaedra traditions.
entries.reading: WHOLE, noting what each character knows at each moment.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 55 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A compact introduction to Roman moral historiography and republican crisis. Its speeches and character portraits reward comparison with Cicero's partisan account.
entries.reading: WHOLE; the conspiracy occurred in 63 BCE.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 56 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. A model of controlled narrative and self-legitimation, crucial for reading conquest critically. Its apparent clarity makes the construction of authority unusually instructive.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: books 1, 6 and 7. Events in Caesar's books concern 58–52 BCE; distinguish Hirtius's continuation.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 57 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Reveals an ancient way of organising rulers through habits, bodies, ancestry and anecdotes. Pairing it with Tacitus teaches differences between biographical and historical explanation.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: Julius Caesar, Augustus and Nero, complete; then Claudius.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 58 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Opens Roman elite society, literary culture and provincial administration through a carefully shaped correspondence. Book 10 changes the evidentiary frame by including exchanges with Trajan.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. L-optional: Latin for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 59 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Expands Greek poetry into rural song, urban voices and learned miniatures. Essential for the pastoral tradition while showing that its founding collection exceeds pastoral alone.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: Idylls 1, 2, 7, 11, 13 and 15.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 60 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Supplies influential divine narratives outside Homer and Hesiod, including Demeter's loss and Apollo's institutions. Attribution to Homer is traditional, not secure authorship.
entries.reading: SELECTIONS: Hymns 2 to Demeter, 3 to Apollo, 4 to Hermes, 5 to Aphrodite and 7 to Dionysus.
entries.caveat: Includes a directly checked primary-text excerpt; scope and other support are specified in the ledger. English translation by default. G-optional: Ancient Greek for original-language philology; not required for the English route.

entries.standing: Position 61 in the owner-supplied Classical Education Top 250. Reworks heroic voyage through learning, uncertain leadership and Medea's psychology. A vital bridge from Homer to Virgil and later narratives of Jason.
entries.reading: WHOLE: four books, after some Homer and Medea.
